Lakota. Also known as the Sioux, they are a Great Plains nation originally spanning the Dakotas, Nebraska, and Montana. Renowned for their horse culture, warrior traditions, and resistance to U.S. expansion, they fought to preserve their buffalo-hunting way of life through leaders like Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse before eventually being confined to reservations.

The Lakota divide into three branches: Lakota in the west, Dakota in the central region, and Nakota in the north. The term "Sioux" is an exonym derived from French renderings of Ojibwe names. After acquiring horses, they became masters of mounted warfare, organizing themselves into bands governed by consensus under hereditary and earned leadership.

Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse led resistance to the Fort Laramie Treaties and the U.S. invasion during the Black Hills gold rush. They defeated Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer at the Battle of Little Bighorn in 1876. The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 had guaranteed the Black Hills as Lakota territory, but the U.S. broke the treaty when gold was discovered in the 1870s.

The Lakota were confined to reservations and subjected to forced assimilation policies, including the Indian Boarding Schools that separated children from families and culture. Today they comprise several federally recognized tribes in South Dakota, North Dakota, Montana, and Nebraska. The Lakota language is still spoken, and revitalization efforts are ongoing. Sitting Bull remains principal among their leaders, while Crazy Horse is famous for an undefeated military career and the Little Bighorn remains their watershed battle of victory.
